extracted.intended_audience: media/communication scholars, students, and researchers interested in internet memes, political communication, and cultural globalization
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and criteria for analyzing how internet memes function politically and circulate across cultures, with attention to form (visual/verbal), functions (persuasion/action/discussion), localization, and subversive strategies under censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and variation turning personal to political
rubrics_metrics.description: “This combination of repetition and variation turns the personal to political: Stories about the sick young woman who is unable to afford medication, the single mom who struggles to provide for her son, and the father who cannot send his daughter to college are reframed as particular cases of the same flawed structure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition of similar personal stories with small variations to reframe private miseries as systemic problems; example: the 'We are the 99 percent' meme collects many individual cases to imply structural economic-political illness. Anti-pattern: isolated anecdotes without thematic repetition fail to generalize or produce political resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes' intertwined functions: persuasion, action, discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: “For the sake of clarity, I have so far differentiated between memes as dealing with persuasion, action, or discussion. Yet my brief analysis has demonstrated that in reality these functions are intertwined: political memes are often used as an amalgamation of all three.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess memes by their persuasive content, their capacity to motivate or enable action, and their role in generating discussion — but expect overlap. Example: the 99 percent meme was persuasive, part of grassroots action, and ignited discussion. Scoring should consider presence of one or multiple functions rather than exclusive categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pop culture as a common ground and shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: “Building on Henry Jenkins’s work... pop culture is used in memes as a common ground to discuss politics. As pop culture is part of people’s everyday lives and cultural identities, using it to talk about politics makes the latter more approachable. For example, Tay describes the heavy usage of Star Wars characters in memes as shorthand to communicate meaning.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective political memes often appropriate recognizable pop-culture references to quickly communicate stance/roles (e.g., politician as Jedi/Palpatine). Example: Obama-as-Luke or Palpatine uttering accusations. Anti-pattern: obscure references that the target audience won't recognize reduce communicative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of depoliticization via pop-culture reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Yet, as demonstrated in chapter 4, this heavy reliance on pop culture images in political memes may, at some points, lead to a process of 'depoliticization,' in which the political and critical aspects of Internet memes are diminished in favor of pure playful amusement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether pop-culture framing preserves or erodes critical political content; playful parody may obscure substantive critique. Warning: high entertainment value can overshadow political message, producing apolitical consumption rather than civic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic photo theme: frontstage–backstage interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: “I found that most political memetic photos relate to a single theme: an interplay between the 'frontstage' and 'backstage' of political performances.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify how images juxtapose public (frontstage) and private/behind-the-scenes (backstage) elements; use Goffman’s distinction to analyze impression management. Example memetic sources: Situation Room photo, Netanyahu–Shalit photo. Anti-pattern: images lacking any sense of performance boundary offer fewer targets for memetic critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontstage/backstage definitions and analytical use
rubrics_metrics.description: “‘Frontstage’ is the main site in which impression management activities are performed... ‘Backstage’ is a more private area, where intimacy, familiarity, and authenticity govern.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these definitions when coding photos: frontstage = projected image for audience; backstage = settings where authenticity/familiarity expected. Memes may strategically expose backstage as staged (not genuine) or relocate backstage into frontstage to critique authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic responses expose inauthenticity/manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: “In their memetic responses to such photos, users expose them as 'inauthentic,' flawed, and manipulated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for meme practices that reveal photo-manipulation, temporal misplacement, or constructed authenticity (e.g., 'Bibi Gump', 'Sarkozy Was There', 'Three Chinese Officials'). Such responses function as grassroots media criticism. Anti-pattern: accepting official framing without interrogating authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes as monitorial-citizen training (spotting manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “These shows [Daily Show/Colbert] provide 'good training grounds for monitorial citizens,' who become accustomed to looking out for signs of manipulation and fabrication. By manipulating political photos, users signal that they are aware of the artificial construction of images and that they can create competing (and somewhat less flattering) images themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess memes for their role in cultivating skeptical, media-literate audiences who detect manipulation; measure how clearly a meme educates viewers about suspicious framing. Example: memes that recontextualize or re-caption official photos to expose spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes expand participatory options and can symbolize democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Memes thus expand the range of participatory options in democracies: citizens can express their political opinions in new and accessible ways... But in nondemocracies, Internet memes are not just about expanding discursive opportunities—they may represent the idea of democracy itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate memes by their accessibility, participatory affordances (ease of remixing, sharing), and symbolic value under repression. In nondemocracies, coded memes may function as public displays of dissent. Consider reach and participatory uptake as metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coded-linguistic strategies to evade censorship (punning and substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: “This ironic usage led to the word being flagged as a sensitive keyword... bloggers and other content creators switched the characters making up the word to produce another phrase... This resulted in a pun, as the new phrase means 'river crab.' Thus, when bloggers write about 'river crab,' or being 'river crabbed,' they are actually talking about censorship.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify linguistic substitutions, puns, homophones, and alternative characters used to circumvent automated censorship; analyze resulting visual memes (e.g., crab with watches). Anti-pattern: literal, uncoded criticism that is easily deleted by censors and thus invisible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of playful audiovisual forms to mask political insults (Grass Mud Horse example)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The 'Grass Mud Horse'... a 'mythical beast' whose name in Chinese is pronounced as literally meaning 'fuck your mother'... the song's sweet facade is deceiving... The harmless beasts represent innocent Internet users... but will prevail.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine use of cute/innocent aesthetics (children’s chorus, alpaca imagery) combined with phonic obscenities as a tactic to denigrate power safely. Note viral derivatives (cartoons, Photoshop, poems) and downstream commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization and commodification of subversive memes
rubrics_metrics.description: “This move from cyberspace to physical artifacts in the 'real world' represents Internet users’ urge to deepen their shared subversive experience. At the same time, the process also signifies the power of capitalism to reinvent itself... the products have already ensured a profit because through free advertising, internet users act voluntarily as marketers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a meme's political potency, consider whether and how commercialization (T-shirts, toys, merchandise) neutralizes or diffuses subversion. Track timeline: initial coded resistance → mainstream commodification. Scoring note: commercialization can be evidence of influence but also dilution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital memes' visual nature: integration with pop culture and polysemy
rubrics_metrics.description: “A further realm of difference between old and new political memes relates to form: digital memes are much more visual than their predecessors. This has two main implications. First, visual display allows greater integration between politics and pop culture. ... A second implication... relates to their polysemic potential—that is, their tendency to be open to multiple readings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess visual memes for intertextual pop-culture cues and for openness to multiple interpretations. Metrics: recognizability of intertext, degree of interpretive ambiguity. Anti-pattern: images with single, narrow reading may mobilize less cross-group discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polysemy amplified by intertextuality
rubrics_metrics.description: “Lillian Boxman-Shabtai claims that this potential for multiple meanings is stronger when visual imagery involves intertextuality: the additional layer of meanings associated with a text such as Star Wars may add complexity and ambiguity to the message.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate how much intertextual references (e.g., Star Wars) add nuanced or conflicting readings. Example: Obama-as-Luke can be read as glorifying or criticizing depending on reader's frame. Use interpretive variance as a feature, not necessarily a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-generated globalization: translation, customization, and invisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “User-generated globalization is a process in which memes are translated, customized, and distributed across the globe by ordinary Internet users... once a text is translated and some local markers are added, its foreign origins may be invisible to those who read and distribute it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze meme diffusion chains for translation and localization practices; identify whether origin is visible or masked. Consider actors (ordinary users vs commercial agents) and non-commercial spread as characteristic. Anti-pattern: treating all global spread as top-down cultural imperialism without tracing grassroots transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of 'global' jokes vs 'translation-resistant' jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: “'Global' jokes tend not to mention specific places or companies... In contrast, translation-resistant jokes tend to focus on specific places within America, on local American stereotypes... Overall, our findings suggest... 'Global' jokes shared two main topics: gender differences and consumerism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify verbal memes by their referential specificity: low-specificity (global) vs high-specificity (local). Evaluate topic content (gender/consumerism likely to travel). For localization scoring, check presence of universal themes and absence of local political references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local adaptation strategies (glocalization): replacing cultural markers
rubrics_metrics.description: “Translations in the three languages explored in detail... incorporated many small local adaptations. Thus, for instance, in the German translations many changes related to sports-oriented references: NBA and rugby were replaced by German indicators such as Fussball-Bundesliga and Sportschau.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing cross-cultural versions, note substitutions of culturally-specific items (sports, brands, institutions). Assess fidelity of joke mechanics vs surface markers: 'ingredients' (stereotypes/mechanism) often remain even if 'flavors' (references) change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features aiding visual/audiovisual meme global spread (simplicity, repetition, whimsy)
rubrics_metrics.description: “This video’s memetic appeal [Gangnam Style] to a combination of simple, repetitive, elements and content that seems (to most non-Korean viewers) completely whimsical and full of puzzling elements. This combination allows, on the one hand, easy imitation... and on the other, incorporation of a very wide arena of themes and topics to its derivatives.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate audiovisual memes for simple, repeatable hooks (dance moves, refrains), whimsical or ambiguous content that invites imitation, and elements that can be easily substituted for local meaning (e.g., 'Gangnam' → 'Mexi Style'). Measure remixability and template potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme format mechanism: top/bottom caption reversal (Successful Black Man)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The 'Successful Black Man' meme features a photo of a young black man... accompanied by two captions: the top line hints at a (usually negative) stereotype associated with being black, while the bottom one reverses it to display a middle-class, responsible family man. The humorous effect of this meme derives from the comic clash between two scripts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the formal comic mechanism (e.g., two-line expectation/subversion). Assess whether reversal punishes reader’s stereotypical reading or reinforces exception-as-rule. Consider social-implication critiques: does the meme challenge stereotypes or implicitly validate them by singling an exception?

rubrics_metrics.name: Format copying vs content/stancial transformation in localization
rubrics_metrics.description: “While the Israeli version copied the format of the American meme, it altered its content and satirical stance... the strong satirical aspect embedded in the original meme seems to get lost in translation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cross-cultural analysis, distinguish between preservation of format and preservation of stance/critique. Scoring should penalize superficial copying that strips satirical edge; reward adaptations that retain or thoughtfully transform underlying critical intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes as polyvocal deliberative spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: “Since meme hubs such as 4chan and Reddit incorporate a variety of contrasting voices and opinions, Internet memes assume a new role in deliberative processes, providing a polyvocal 'meeting space' between opposing camps. In this sense, they differ from political jokes, often told in intimate gatherings with like-minded others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a meme fosters cross-cutting dialogue across communities (polyvocality) versus preaching to the converted. Metrics: diversity of participating platforms, presence of opposing readings, and cross-group sharing. Anti-pattern: memes that circulate only within echo chambers.
